newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan vehicle output set to pull out of 5-yr skid.
newsitem.headline: Japan vehicle output set to pull out of 5-yr skid.

text.p: Japan's vehicle production jumped for a second successive month in October and output for the year is likely to climb, pulling out of a five-year skid, a manufacturers' group said on Monday.

Vehicle production in October rose 12.3 percent from the same month last year to 941,461 vehicles, boosted by strong domestic demand and revived exports, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association said.

"Japan's annual vehicle production in 1996 will exceed the level of 1995 because domestic demand still remains strong and the export environment has improved because of the weaker yen," an association official said.
Vehicle production in 1995 fell 3.4 percent from the year before to 10.2 million units, marking the fifth straight year of decline.

In the first 10 months of 1996, domestic production totalled 8.57 million vehicles, up 0.1 percent over the same period last year. The association said the gains would continue in the last two months of the year because of the weaker yen and stronger domestic demand.
It said domestic demand in October rose 5.8 percent from October last year to 575,672 vehicles.
It estimated exports for October would be up 17 percent from a year earlier. Official export figures will be announced on Thursday.
The yen stood at around 112 yen to the dollar on Monday, compared with about 100 yen a year ago. The cheaper yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets.
All Japanese automobile manufacturers, except Nissan Motor Co Ltd and Isuzu Motors Ltd, produced more vehicles in October, mainly because of strong demand for new recreational vehicles.
Toyota Motor Corp's output jumped 20.2 percent to 337,181 vehicles, while that of Honda Motor Co Ltd rose 40.3 percent and Mitsubishi Motors Corp's was up 6.2 percent.
Domestic demand for Nissan cars was slow because a "new model effect" wore off several models introduced last year.
Isuzu had lower exports in October due to the effects of a consumer magazine report in the United States in mid-September, a company spokesman said.
The report said tests showed that Isuzu's Trooper could roll over when the vehicle was turned sharply, for instance, to avoid an unexpected obstacle.
But Isuzu Motors America Inc said the tests were flawed and that demand for the Trooper was rebounding, the Isuzu spokesman said.
